lessons.title: From Peer to Boss
lessons.summary: Handle the first weeks after being promoted over your former colleagues. You will learn how to reset relationships, set fair boundaries and earn credibility without trying to prove yourself overnight.

sections.heading: What actually changes on day one
sections.body:
Yesterday you were judged on your own work. From today you are judged on what your team delivers. That is the real shift, and it is bigger than the new title or the extra ₹8,000 in your salary.

Take Priya, who was promoted to team lead in a Pune operations team where she had worked alongside six colleagues for three years. On her first Monday nothing looked different: same desk, same chai break, same WhatsApp group. But now she approves leave, reviews errors and speaks for the team in her manager's meetings. Her old friends noticed the change before she did.

Accept that the relationship has changed, even if you wish it had not. Pretending you are "still just one of the gang" usually ends with you avoiding hard decisions or making them in a way that looks unfair.
do: Tell yourself clearly: my job is now the team's results
Expect some awkwardness and treat it as normal
dont: Pretend nothing has changed to stay popular

sections.heading: Have the reset conversation early
sections.body:
In your first two weeks, have a short one-to-one talk with each former peer. Do not wait for problems to appear. Keep it simple and honest: "I know this is a change for both of us. I value working with you, and I'd like to hear what would make this team work better and what you need from me."

Then listen more than you talk. Note what they say and follow up on at least one point within a week, so they see the conversation was not a formality.

If someone else also applied for the role, speak to them first and privately. Acknowledge it without being awkward: "I know you were interested in this role too. Your experience matters to this team, and I'd like us to work well together. What would be useful to you right now?" Do not apologise for being chosen, and do not avoid them.
do: Meet every former peer one-to-one within two weeks
Follow up on something each person raised
dont: Ignore the colleague who also wanted the job
Apologise for getting the promotion

sections.heading: Friendship, fairness and boundaries
sections.body:
You can stay friendly with old colleagues. What changes is that you must be fair to everyone and be seen to be fair. If your closest friend gets the easy client and the early leave approvals, the rest of the team will notice within days.

A few boundaries help. Do not join gossip about other team members or criticise senior management in the team group. Do not share confidential information, such as appraisal ratings or restructuring plans, with friends. Have lunch or chai with different people, not only your old circle.

If a friend tests the line ("Arre, just mark me present, no one will check"), say no warmly but clearly: "I can't do that for anyone, including you. Let's see if we can adjust your shift instead."
do: Apply the same rules to friends and everyone else
Keep confidential information confidential
dont: Vent about your manager to your old peer group
Give friends the best work by default

sections.heading: Stop being the team's best individual worker
sections.body:
Many new managers keep doing their old job because it feels safe and they are good at it. They take the toughest cases, fix every error themselves and stay late. The result is a tired manager and a team that never grows.

Shift your time deliberately. A practical rule for the first months: spend less than half your day on your own tasks, and the rest on planning, coaching, unblocking and talking to your manager and other teams. If you catch yourself redoing someone's work, stop and ask what they need to do it right next time.

Your new skills, such as delegating, giving feedback and running one-on-ones, will feel slower than doing it yourself at first. That is normal; the payoff comes over weeks, not hours.
do: Block time every week for coaching and planning
dont: Quietly redo team members' work at night

sections.heading: Earn credibility in your first 90 days
sections.body:
Resist the urge to change everything in week one. Spend the first few weeks listening. Ask each person three questions: what should we keep doing, what should we stop, and what should we start?

Then pick one or two small, visible improvements the team itself asked for, such as fixing a confusing handover sheet or getting a broken printer replaced, and deliver them. Small promises kept build more trust than big speeches.

Admit what you do not know. "I haven't handled vendor escalations before. Rahul, you've done this for two years; can you walk me through it?" shows confidence, not weakness. Finally, agree with your own manager on what success looks like at 30, 60 and 90 days, so you are not guessing.
do: Ask: keep, stop, start
Deliver one or two quick wins the team asked for
dont: Announce sweeping changes in your first week

takeaways: Your success is now measured by your team's results, not your own output.
Hold a short reset conversation with each former peer in your first two weeks.
Stay friendly, but apply the same rules to everyone and keep confidences.
Spend less time doing and more time planning, coaching and unblocking.
Listen first, then deliver small wins the team asked for.
quiz: You have just been promoted over five colleagues. What is the most useful first step?
Announce a new set of team rules on day one so everyone knows you are now in charge
Hold short one-to-one conversations with each of them in the first two weeks
Carry on exactly as before and wait for any problems to surface on their own
Ask your manager to announce any changes so you can avoid awkward conversations
Early one-to-ones reset the relationship and show you want to listen before you act.
Ankit also applied for your new role. How should you handle it?
Avoid the topic completely so that he does not feel embarrassed in front of others
Apologise to him and say the final decision was not really in your hands
Give him lighter work for a few weeks so that he has time to get over it
Speak to him privately first, acknowledge it and ask what would help
Acknowledging it directly and respectfully is better than avoidance, apology or special treatment.
Your closest friend on the team asks you to approve leave that clashes with a peak week, which you have refused others. What should you do?
Decline, explain the rule is the same for everyone, and suggest another date
Approve it quietly, because she has supported you loyally for many years
Approve it, but ask her not to mention the approval to anyone else on the team
Ask the whole team to vote on whether she should be given the leave
Being seen to be fair matters more than ever once you manage former peers.
Which behaviour most damages a new manager's credibility with the team?
Admitting they have never handled a particular process before
Asking the team what they would keep, stop and start
Joining the team's group chat to complain about senior management
Taking a few weeks to listen before changing processes
Criticising leadership with the team undermines your role and models the wrong behaviour.
You notice you are staying late every day redoing your team's reports. What is the better approach?
Keep going, because a manager should personally guarantee the quality of every report
Find out what each person needs to get it right and coach them on it
Stop checking the reports altogether and let mistakes reach the client
Ask HR to replace the people who keep making mistakes
Coaching builds the team's ability; redoing work keeps you stuck as an individual contributor.
In your first month, what kind of change is best to make?
A complete restructure of who handles which clients and regions
A new strict attendance policy to set the tone early
Nothing at all for six months, to avoid upsetting anyone
A small, visible fix that the team itself asked for
A quick win the team wanted builds trust; big changes work better once you have listened.
A former peer jokes, "Now that you're the boss, you won't have chai with us anymore." What is a good response?
"Of course — and I'll make time for the whole team, not just us."
"Things are different now, so I'll need to keep some distance from all of you."
"Don't worry, nothing at all has changed between us, I promise."
Ignore the comment and quickly change the subject to work
It keeps the friendship while signalling fairness to the whole team.
What should you agree with your own manager early on?
Which team members you can leave alone because they need no attention
What success looks like for you at 30, 60 and 90 days
That you will keep personally handling every escalation yourself
That they will deliver any bad news to your team on your behalf
Clear expectations stop you from guessing what you are being judged on.
A friend on the team asks what appraisal rating a colleague received. What do you say?
Tell them, since everyone will find out about it eventually anyway
Hint at the rating without saying the exact number, so no rule is broken
Say you can't share anyone's rating, just as you wouldn't share theirs
Ask them why they want to know, then decide
Confidential information stays confidential, whatever the friendship.
Which statement best describes the main shift from peer to manager?
You now need to be the most technically skilled person on the team
You should stop being friendly with anyone who reports to you
You must make every decision alone to show your authority
You are now judged mainly on what the team delivers
The core change is that your results come through other people.

scenarios.title: The colleague who wanted your job
scenarios.situation: You and Sneha both interviewed for the team lead role in your Bengaluru branch, and you got it. Since the announcement she has been quiet in meetings and answers your messages in one word. Two important client reviews are coming up next week.

options.text: Ask Sneha for a private chat: "I know you wanted this role too. Your client knowledge is a big strength for us. How can we work well together, and what would be useful for you?"
options.feedback: It acknowledges the situation honestly, values her and opens a two-way conversation before the pressure of the reviews.

options.text: Give Sneha space for a few weeks and assign the client reviews to someone else.
options.feedback: Avoiding her and sidelining her work can feel like punishment and makes the distance worse.

options.text: Mention in the team meeting that everyone needs to support the new structure.
options.feedback: A public, general message does not address the real issue and may embarrass her.

options.text: Ask Sneha to lead one of the client reviews and check in with her afterwards about how things are going.
options.feedback: Trusting her with important work is positive, but without an honest conversation first the tension may stay unspoken.

scenarios.title: The friend who wants a favour
scenarios.situation: Your close friend Karan, now in your team, logged in two hours late after a wedding. He messages you: "Bhai, just mark it as work from home, please. No one will know." Others on the team have been marked late for similar delays this month.

options.text: Mark it as work from home just this once, since it was a family function.
options.feedback: Bending rules for a friend is exactly what makes a team feel the new manager is unfair.

options.text: Reply: "I can't mark it differently for anyone, including you. Let's apply for half-day leave, and next time tell me in advance so we can plan."
options.feedback: It is warm but firm, applies the same rule to everyone and offers a practical alternative.

options.text: Refuse, and remind him in front of the team that rules apply to all.
options.feedback: The decision is right but doing it publicly embarrasses him unnecessarily.

options.text: Refuse by message and leave it there.
options.feedback: Correct decision, but offering an alternative and a way to avoid it next time keeps the relationship stronger.

scenarios.title: The temptation to fix it yourself
scenarios.situation: It is 7 pm. A monthly MIS report from your team member Divya has formatting errors and two wrong totals. It is due to the regional office at 10 am. You could fix it yourself in 40 minutes.

options.text: Fix it tonight without telling Divya, so the report goes on time.
options.feedback: The report is saved but Divya never learns, and you will be fixing it again next month.

options.text: Fix the totals tonight so the deadline is met, then sit with Divya tomorrow to go through the errors and agree a checking routine.
options.feedback: It protects the deadline and turns the mistake into coaching so it does not recur.

options.text: Send it back to Divya tonight and ask her to correct it before 10 am.
options.feedback: It keeps ownership with her, but it may not be fair to expect late-night work without warning, and coaching is still needed.

cards.title: From peer to boss
cards.text: Yesterday you were judged on your own work. Today you're judged on your team's results. In the next two minutes, learn how to make that jump without losing trust.

cards.title: Have the reset conversation
cards.text: Meet each former peer one-to-one in your first two weeks. Listen more than you talk.
cards.bad: Hi all, I'm the lead now. Let's keep things the same.
cards.good: This is a change for both of us. What would make this team work better, and what do you need from me?

cards.title: Talk to the one who also applied
cards.text: Speak to them first and privately. Acknowledge it, value their experience, and don't apologise or avoid them.
cards.example: I know you wanted this role too. Your experience matters here. What would help you right now?

cards.title: Friendly, but fair to all
cards.text: Friends still get the same rules as everyone. Say no warmly and offer an option.
cards.bad: Okay, I'll mark you present. Just don't tell anyone.
cards.good: I can't do that for anyone, including you. Let's adjust your shift instead.

cards.title: Stop redoing their work
cards.text: Fixing everything yourself feels safe, but your team never grows. Coach instead.
cards.bad: Staying late every night to quietly correct the team's reports.
cards.good: Fix today's urgent error, then sit with the person to agree how to catch it next time.

cards.title: Your first 90 days
cards.text: Tap each one as you plan it.
items: Ask everyone: keep, stop, start?
Deliver one small fix the team asked for
Admit what you don't know and ask experts
Agree 30-60-90 day goals with your manager
cards.tip: Hold off on big changes until you have listened.

cards.title: You've got it!
cards.text: Five ideas for your first weeks as a manager:

lessons.title: Delegating Well
lessons.summary: Decide what to hand over, brief people so they can deliver, and check progress without micromanaging. You will learn a simple briefing structure and how to match the level of freedom to the person.

sections.heading: Why new managers hold on too tightly
sections.body:
Most first-time managers delegate too little, not too much. The usual reasons sound sensible: "It's faster if I do it", "They'll make mistakes", "I don't want to burden them." Each one is true for a single task and wrong over a quarter.

If a weekly report takes you one hour and teaching someone takes three hours once, you get your time back within a month. More importantly, your team learns. People who are never given stretch work stop growing, get bored and start looking at job portals.

A useful test: list everything you did last week. Mark tasks only you can do (such as appraisals or decisions your manager expects from you), tasks someone else could do with a little help, and tasks someone already could do. The second and third lists are your delegation candidates.
do: List last week's tasks and sort them into three groups
dont: Keep a task only because you enjoy it or are good at it

sections.heading: Choose the right task for the right person
sections.body:
Delegation is not dumping. Handing over only the boring work tells people you see them as spare hands. Mix routine tasks with work that builds a skill the person wants, such as presenting to a client or analysing data.

Match the task to both ability and interest. Ritu, who is great with Excel and wants to move into analytics, is a natural fit for building the new dashboard. Faizan, who is new, might start by preparing the data for it while Ritu designs it.

Be careful with tasks that carry high risk, such as a key client renewal or anything involving compliance sign-off. You can still delegate parts of these, but stay closer and agree checkpoints.
do: Link delegated work to someone's growth goals
Delegate parts of high-risk work with closer checkpoints
dont: Give away only the dull tasks
Delegate a task you cannot explain clearly yourself

sections.heading: Brief so people can actually deliver
sections.body:
Most delegation fails at the handover. "Can you look into the vendor issue?" leaves the person guessing what, why, by when and how much freedom they have.

A good brief covers five things. The outcome: what finished looks like. The why: how it fits the bigger goal. The deadline and checkpoints. The authority: what they can decide alone and what needs your approval, including any spending limit. The resources: people, files and past examples.

Before: "Handle the Diwali gifting for clients."
After: "Could you own Diwali gifting for our top 40 clients? Goal is to have gifts delivered by 25 October. Budget is ₹1,500 per client; you can choose the vendor yourself under that. Last year's list and feedback are in the shared drive. Let's review your shortlist on Friday."

Finish by asking them to play it back in their own words. "Just so we're aligned, how are you planning to approach it?" catches misunderstandings early.
do: Cover outcome, why, deadline, authority and resources
Ask them to play back the plan
dont: Hand over work in a corridor with one vague line

sections.heading: Match the freedom to the person
sections.body:
There is no single right level of control. Think of a range. At one end: "Do it exactly this way and check with me at each step." In the middle: "Recommend an approach, and go ahead once I agree." At the other end: "Handle it and update me when it's done."

New joiners and new tasks need the first end. Experienced people on familiar work need the last. Problems come when the level does not match: a fresher left alone flounders, while a senior person checked hourly feels insulted.

Say the level out loud so there is no guessing: "For this one, decide the vendor yourself; just loop me in before you sign anything above ₹50,000."
do: State the level of freedom explicitly
dont: Use the same level of control for everyone

sections.heading: Follow up without micromanaging
sections.body:
Agree checkpoints at the start, then use them. A five-minute check on Friday is support; messaging "Any update?" three times a day is micromanagement.

When something goes wrong, resist taking the task back. Ask: "What's blocking you?" and "What options do you see?" Offer help, but leave ownership with them unless the risk is serious.

When the work is done, give credit in public. "Ritu built this dashboard" in the regional review costs you nothing and tells the whole team that delegated work is valued.
do: Use agreed checkpoints
Credit the person who did the work
dont: Take the task back at the first problem
Present delegated work as your own

takeaways: Delegating takes time upfront and saves far more later.
Mix routine tasks with work that helps people grow.
Brief with outcome, why, deadline, authority and resources.
Say clearly how much freedom the person has.
Check in at agreed points and give public credit.
quiz: Which is the best brief for delegating a task?
"Please look into the vendor issue whenever you get some free time over the next week or so."
"Sort out the vendor thing for me; you already know what needs to be done."
"Compare three vendors, recommend one by Thursday; you can approve up to ₹50,000."
"Do whatever you think is right about the vendors; no need to update me."
It names the outcome, deadline and limit of authority.
A new joiner is handling a client report for the first time. What level of freedom fits best?
Clear steps and checkpoints, with you available for questions
Full freedom, so that they learn by figuring everything out on their own
None at all; you should quietly do the report yourself this time
Full freedom, but you redo the report yourself before it goes out
New people on new tasks need more structure; freedom grows with experience.
Which reason for not delegating is usually the weakest over a few months?
The task involves an appraisal decision only you can make
"It's faster if I just do it myself."
The task needs your manager's specific approval
It's a confidential salary review
It is faster once, but teaching someone saves far more time over weeks.
You delegate only data entry and photocopying to your team. What is the likely result?
People feel trusted with important work
The team develops new skills quickly
Your own workload drops to a healthy level
People feel used as spare hands and lose motivation
Delegation should include growth tasks, not only dull ones.
Halfway through, your team member hits a problem with the delegated task. What should you do first?
Ask what is blocking them and what options they see
Take the task back immediately so it gets done properly
Tell them to work it out without your help
Reassign it to someone more experienced
Coaching keeps ownership with them while helping them move forward.
Why ask the person to play back the plan in their own words?
To test whether they were paying attention during the briefing
To have a record in case things go wrong
To catch misunderstandings before work starts
To make the meeting last longer
Playback is a quick check that you are both picturing the same outcome.
An experienced colleague is handling a routine task she has done for years. You message her every two hours for updates. What is the likely effect?
She feels supported and appreciated
She feels mistrusted and micromanaged
The quality of her work goes up
It has no effect, since she is experienced
Experienced people on familiar work need freedom, not constant checking.
Which task is best kept closer to you, with tight checkpoints, even if parts are delegated?
Ordering stationery for the branch
Updating the team leave calendar
Booking the venue for the team lunch
Preparing a compliance sign-off for a key client
High-risk work can be delegated in parts, but needs closer oversight.
Your team member built the dashboard that impressed the regional head. What should you say in the review?
"Our team built this dashboard."
"I built this dashboard with some help from the team."
Say nothing about who did it
"Ritu built this; she'll walk you through it."
Naming the person builds trust and shows that delegated work is valued.
What is the main purpose of stating the level of authority when delegating?
So the person knows what they can decide alone and what needs approval
So that you have someone to blame if anything goes wrong with the work later
So HR has a formal written record of who was given the task
So the person feels pressure and works faster to finish it
Clear authority prevents both over-checking and costly surprises.

scenarios.title: The vague handover
scenarios.situation: You are a team lead at a Hyderabad IT services firm. Your manager has asked you to organise a client visit next month. You are stretched and want to hand it to Meera, who has been on the team for a year and has never organised one.

options.text: Tell Meera in passing: "Can you take care of the client visit next month?"
options.feedback: Without outcome, budget, authority or checkpoints, Meera is left guessing and likely to miss something.

options.text: Brief Meera on the goal, date, budget and what she can book herself, share last year's plan, ask her to play it back and agree a check-in on Friday.
options.feedback: A complete brief plus playback and a checkpoint suits someone doing this for the first time.

options.text: Write a detailed step-by-step checklist and ask Meera to follow it exactly without changes.
options.feedback: Structure helps a first-timer, but explaining the why and inviting her ideas would build more ownership.

options.text: Organise it yourself; it's quicker than explaining.
options.feedback: It saves time once but keeps you overloaded and gives Meera no chance to grow.

scenarios.title: The senior who feels watched
scenarios.situation: Rakesh has handled vendor payments for eight years. Since you became his manager three months ago, you have reviewed every payment file before release. He tells you, "Do you not trust my work?"

options.text: Explain that you are new and need to see everything for now; he should not take it personally.
options.feedback: Honest, but it does not set an end date or a plan for moving to lighter checks.

options.text: Thank him for saying it, agree to move to spot checks plus approval only above an agreed amount, and review the arrangement in a month.
options.feedback: It matches oversight to his experience while keeping sensible control on high-value items.

options.text: Stop reviewing his files altogether from today.
options.feedback: Swinging from full control to none removes even reasonable checks on payments.

scenarios.title: The stalled project
scenarios.situation: You delegated a customer-feedback survey to Imran, a fresher. A week before the deadline he has collected only 30 of 200 responses and looks stressed. Your manager is asking for the results.

options.text: Take the survey back and finish it yourself over the weekend.
options.feedback: It solves this deadline but tells Imran he failed and teaches him nothing.

options.text: Sit with Imran, ask what is blocking responses, help him pick two new ways to reach customers and agree daily five-minute check-ins until the deadline.
options.feedback: It keeps ownership with him, adds support and increases checkpoints to match the risk.

options.text: Tell your manager the deadline will slip because Imran is struggling.
options.feedback: Blaming a team member to your manager damages trust; it is your job to support and manage the risk.

options.text: Ask a senior colleague to help Imran collect the remaining responses.
options.feedback: Extra help may work, but without understanding the blocker the same problem may recur.

cards.title: Delegate like a manager
cards.text: Most new managers hold on to too much work. Learn how to hand tasks over so they actually get done — and your team grows in the process.

cards.title: Slower once, faster forever
cards.text: List last week's tasks. Mark what only you can do. Everything else is a delegation candidate.
cards.example: A one-hour weekly report that takes three hours to teach pays you back within a month.

cards.title: Delegation is not dumping
cards.text: Mix routine tasks with work that builds a skill the person wants.
cards.bad: Giving Ritu only data entry and photocopying.
cards.good: Asking Ritu, who wants to move into analytics, to build the new dashboard.

cards.title: Brief so they can deliver
cards.text: Cover outcome, why, deadline, authority and resources.
cards.bad: Handle the Diwali gifting for clients.
cards.good: Own Diwali gifting for our top 40 clients, delivered by 25 Oct. Budget ₹1,500 each; choose the vendor yourself. Let's review your shortlist Friday.

cards.title: Say how much freedom
cards.text: New task or new person: more structure. Experienced and familiar: more freedom. Say it out loud.
cards.bad: Checking every payment file of someone who has done it for eight years.
cards.good: Decide the vendor yourself; loop me in before signing anything above ₹50,000.

cards.title: After you hand it over
cards.text: Tap each one as you do it.
items: Ask them to play back the plan
Check in only at agreed points
If stuck, ask what's blocking them
Credit them by name when it's done
cards.tip: Resist taking the task back at the first problem.

cards.title: You've got it!
cards.text: Five habits for your next handover:

lessons.title: Giving Feedback as a Manager
lessons.summary: Give specific praise, useful corrective feedback and handle difficult conversations calmly. You will learn a simple situation-behaviour-impact structure and phrases you can use the same day.

sections.heading: Feedback is part of the job, not an extra
sections.body:
Many new managers avoid feedback because it feels awkward, especially with people who were recently their peers. So they save it all for the annual appraisal. The result is a team member who hears in March about a problem that started in July, and feels ambushed.

Good managers give small, frequent feedback, both positive and corrective, close to the moment it happens. A two-minute conversation on Tuesday about Monday's client call is more useful than a paragraph in a review form months later.

Aim for a healthy balance. If the only time people hear from you is when something goes wrong, they will start to dread your messages. If you only ever praise, your praise loses value and real problems grow.
do: Give feedback within a day or two of the event
Give both recognition and correction regularly
dont: Save all feedback for the annual appraisal

sections.heading: Use situation, behaviour, impact
sections.body:
Vague feedback does not help. "Good job" and "You need to be more professional" leave the person unsure what to repeat or change. A simple structure fixes this: describe the situation, the specific behaviour you saw, and its impact.

Corrective example. Before: "You're always careless with client data." After: "In yesterday's update to the Mehta account (situation), the spreadsheet had last quarter's figures (behaviour). The client noticed and asked whether our other numbers were reliable (impact)."

Then move to the future with a question: "What could help you catch this before sending?" Listen to their answer. Often they already know the fix, and a solution they choose is one they will follow.

Describe behaviour, not personality. "You interrupted Neha twice in the meeting" can be discussed; "You're arrogant" only starts an argument.
do: Name the situation, behaviour and impact
Ask what they would do differently
dont: Use words like "always", "never" or personality labels

sections.heading: Recognition that actually means something
sections.body:
Praise works best when it is specific and sincere. "Great work, team!" in the WhatsApp group is pleasant but forgettable. "Aarti, the way you calmed down that customer and still collected the documents saved us a complaint. That's exactly the approach I want us to use" tells Aarti and everyone else what good looks like.

Use the same situation-behaviour-impact structure for praise. Recognise effort and good judgement, not only results; someone who followed the right process on a deal that fell through still deserves credit.

Ask people how they like to be recognised. Some enjoy a mention in the team meeting; others would rather get a quiet message or a note to your manager. Make sure recognition is shared fairly and not only to the most visible or vocal people.
do: Make praise specific
Recognise good judgement as well as results
dont: Praise only the loudest performers

sections.heading: Correcting in private, and in the right setting
sections.body:
Recognition can be public; correction should almost always be private. Pointing out someone's mistake in front of the team, or in a group chat, makes them defensive and damages trust for everyone watching.

Choose the moment. Do not give difficult feedback just before someone presents to a client or as they are leaving for the day. A quiet meeting room or a call with video on works far better than a long text message, where tone is easily misread.

Keep it short and focused on one or two points. A list of twelve complaints overwhelms people, and they will remember none of it.
do: Correct in private, face to face or on a call
dont: Criticise someone in a team meeting or group chat
Give feedback by long text message

sections.heading: Handling a difficult conversation
sections.body:
Some conversations are harder: repeated missed deadlines, behaviour that upsets colleagues, or performance that is putting a target at risk. Prepare for these. Write down the facts with dates, the impact, and what change you need to see.

Open directly and calmly: "I want to talk about the last three deadlines that were missed, because it is affecting the client." Then stop and listen. There may be a reason you do not know about, such as a health issue or a problem at home. Show care without dropping the expectation: "I'm sorry you're dealing with that. Let's work out what support helps, and what we can realistically commit to."

End with clear next steps and a follow-up date, and write a short summary afterwards. If the issue involves harassment, discrimination or anything that may breach company policy, involve HR rather than handling it alone.
do: Prepare facts, impact and the change you need
Agree next steps and a follow-up date
dont: Go in without preparing
Handle policy breaches like harassment alone

takeaways: Give small, frequent feedback close to the event.
Use situation, behaviour, impact — then ask what they'd do differently.
Make praise specific, sincere and fairly shared.
Praise in public; correct in private.
Prepare for difficult conversations and end with clear next steps.
quiz: Which is the most useful corrective feedback?
"You need to be more careful with your work, especially with the client reports."
"In Monday's Mehta update the figures were last quarter's, and the client doubted our accuracy."
"You're always making silly mistakes in reports and it reflects badly on us."
"Please improve your attention to detail going forward, as this keeps happening with client work."
It names the situation, behaviour and impact, so the person knows exactly what to fix.
Your team member made an error in a report two months ago. When is the best time to give feedback about a mistake like this in future?
Within a day or two of it happening
At the next quarterly review
Only if it happens three more times
In the annual appraisal, with examples
Feedback close to the event is clearer and avoids people feeling ambushed later.
Which praise is most effective?
"Great job, everyone!" in the team group
"You're a superstar."
"Aarti, calming that customer and still collecting the documents saved us a complaint."
"Keep it up, nice work."
Specific praise shows the person and the team what good looks like.
Where should you point out a team member's mistake?
In the team meeting so others learn from it
In the team WhatsApp group so there is a record
In an email copied to your manager
Privately, either in person or on a call
Private correction avoids embarrassment and defensiveness.
After describing the problem, what is a good next step?
Tell them exactly how they must fix it, step by step
Ask what they think could help prevent it next time
List other mistakes they have made over the past year
End the meeting quickly to avoid discomfort
People commit more to solutions they help create.
Which statement describes behaviour rather than personality?
"You're arrogant in meetings."
"You have a bad attitude."
"You're too lazy about follow-ups."
"You interrupted Neha twice while she was presenting."
Specific behaviour can be discussed and changed; labels start arguments.
A team member followed the right process, but the client still chose a competitor. What should you do?
Recognise the good judgement and process, and review what you can learn
Say nothing about it, since the deal was lost in the end anyway
Remind them that in this business only final results really matter to anyone
Praise them publicly for winning the client
Recognising good process encourages the right behaviour even when results vary.
In a difficult conversation about missed deadlines, your team member mentions a family health issue. What is the best response?
Drop the topic completely and never raise it again
Say personal issues should not affect work
Show care, discuss support, and agree realistic commitments
Ask for medical proof before continuing
Empathy and clear expectations can go together.
A team member reports that a colleague is making repeated offensive remarks about her. What should you do?
Tell her to ignore the remarks and focus on her own work
Handle it yourself quietly without informing anyone else at all
Ask the two of them to sort it out together
Take it seriously and involve HR as per company policy
Possible harassment or policy breaches need HR involvement, not informal handling alone.
How many issues should you usually raise in a single feedback conversation?
One or two focused, specific points
Every issue you have noticed this year
As many as you can fit into the time
None — let them raise issues themselves
Focused feedback is remembered and acted on; long lists overwhelm.

scenarios.title: The late but talented performer
scenarios.situation: Vikram is your strongest analyst in a Gurugram fintech, but he has submitted three of the last four weekly reports a day late. The delay means your manager gets numbers after her Monday meeting. Vikram is well liked, and you used to be his peer.

options.text: Mention in the team meeting that "some people" need to submit reports on time.
options.feedback: Indirect public hints confuse everyone and do not address Vikram's specific issue.

options.text: Meet Vikram privately: name the three late reports and the impact on Monday's meeting, ask what's getting in the way, and agree a plan and a check-in.
options.feedback: Specific, private, two-way and future-focused — it addresses the issue while respecting him.

options.text: Send Vikram a message: "Please make sure reports are on time from now on."
options.feedback: It is clear and private, but a text message misses the impact and the chance to understand the cause.

options.text: Let it go because his analysis is excellent and you don't want to spoil the relationship.
options.feedback: Avoiding feedback lets the problem grow and is unfair to others who meet deadlines.

scenarios.title: Recognising the quiet contributor
scenarios.situation: Your team just closed a difficult quarter. In the review call, your manager praises Siddharth, who presented the results. You know that Lakshmi quietly built the entire data model that made the analysis possible.

options.text: Say in the call: "Siddharth presented it well, and Lakshmi built the data model behind it — that's what made the analysis possible."
options.feedback: It credits both people fairly and specifically, in front of the audience that matters.

options.text: Send Lakshmi a private thank-you message after the call.
options.feedback: Kind and sincere, but your manager still does not know about her contribution.

options.text: Stay quiet; Lakshmi probably prefers not to be in the spotlight.
options.feedback: Assuming without asking means her work stays invisible; recognition should be fairly shared.

scenarios.title: Feedback right before a client meeting
scenarios.situation: You noticed in the morning that Pooja's client presentation has a few weak slides. She is presenting to an important client in 20 minutes and is already nervous.

options.text: Go through every weakness in detail now so she can fix them.
options.feedback: A long critique minutes before a presentation shakes confidence and leaves no time to fix much.

options.text: Point out one quick, fixable issue if it is critical, wish her luck, and schedule a fuller review after the meeting.
options.feedback: It protects her confidence, fixes anything critical and saves the detailed feedback for the right time.

options.text: Say nothing now and give feedback after the meeting.
options.feedback: Good timing for detailed feedback, but if one issue could embarrass her with the client, a quick flag now helps.

cards.title: Feedback that helps people grow
cards.text: Feedback is part of a manager's job, not an extra. Learn how to praise, correct and handle tough talks so people actually improve.

cards.title: Small and often beats once a year
cards.text: Give feedback within a day or two. Nobody should first hear about a July problem in their March appraisal.
cards.example: Two minutes on Tuesday about Monday's client call.

cards.title: Situation, behaviour, impact
cards.text: Be specific, then ask: what could help next time?
cards.bad: You're always careless with client data.
cards.good: In yesterday's Mehta update, the figures were last quarter's. The client asked if our other numbers are reliable.

cards.title: Make praise specific
cards.text: Use the same structure for recognition. Notice good judgement, not only results.
cards.good: Aarti, calming that customer and still collecting the documents saved us a complaint.

cards.title: Behaviour, not personality
cards.text: Labels start arguments. Behaviour can be discussed and changed.
cards.good: You interrupted Neha twice while she was presenting.

cards.title: Praise in public, correct in private
cards.text: Never correct someone in a team meeting or group chat. Use a quiet room or a video call, not a long text.
cards.example: Raise one or two points, not twelve.

cards.title: Before a difficult conversation
cards.text: Tap each one as you prepare.
items: Facts with dates
The impact on clients or the team
The change you need to see
Next steps and a follow-up date
cards.tip: Harassment or policy breach? Involve HR.

cards.title: You've got it!
cards.text: Five habits for your next feedback chat:

lessons.title: Running Useful One-on-Ones
lessons.summary: Run regular one-on-ones that your team finds useful rather than a status check. You will learn how to set a rhythm, use good questions and follow through on what you hear.

sections.heading: What a one-on-one is for
sections.body:
A one-on-one is a short, regular meeting between you and one team member. Its main purpose is not to collect status updates; you can get those from a tracker or a standup. It is the person's time to raise concerns, get help, discuss growth and build a working relationship with you.

Think of it as preventive maintenance. Small issues, such as confusion about priorities, friction with a colleague or a growing interest in another role, surface early here instead of turning into a resignation letter.

A useful rule of thumb: the team member should do most of the talking. If you speak for 25 minutes of a 30-minute slot, it has become your meeting, not theirs.
do: Treat it as their meeting more than yours
dont: Turn it into a project status update

sections.heading: Set a rhythm and protect it
sections.body:
Weekly or fortnightly, for 20 to 30 minutes, works for most teams. Larger teams may need fortnightly; new joiners often benefit from weekly in their first months. Pick a regular slot and put it in both calendars as a recurring meeting.

The most common mistake is cancelling. When a manager moves the one-on-one three times in a row for "something urgent", the message received is "you are not a priority." If you must reschedule, move it rather than cancel, and say why.

In hybrid or field teams, a video call works well. For sales staff on the road, a fixed call slot on the way back from client visits can work. Keep cameras on where possible, and avoid doing it while driving or checking email.
do: Use a recurring slot in both calendars
Reschedule rather than cancel
dont: Cancel repeatedly for "urgent" work
Check your phone during the meeting

sections.heading: A simple structure
sections.body:
A light structure stops one-on-ones from becoming either aimless chat or a lecture. A shared document with a running list of topics helps; either person can add points during the week.

One easy flow for 30 minutes: first, their topics (about 15 minutes). Then your topics, such as feedback or upcoming changes (about 10 minutes). Finally, actions: who will do what by when (about 5 minutes).

Every few weeks, set aside a session for longer-term topics: career goals, skills they want to build, or how they feel about their workload. These conversations rarely happen unless you plan for them.
do: Keep a shared running agenda
End with clear actions and owners
dont: Skip career conversations because "there's no time"

sections.heading: Questions that open people up
sections.body:
"Everything okay?" almost always gets "Yes, all good." Better questions are specific and open. Try a few of these, not all at once.

"What's taking up most of your energy this week?"
"Is anything slowing you down that I could help remove?"
"What's one thing I could do differently as your manager?"
"Which part of your work do you enjoy most right now, and which least?"
"Where would you like to be in a year, and what would help you get there?"

After asking, wait. Silence of a few seconds is fine; people often say the most important thing after a pause. When feedback about you comes, thank them and do not argue, even if you disagree. If you get defensive once, you may not hear honest feedback again.
do: Ask open, specific questions
Pause and let them think
dont: Ask only "Everything okay?"
Argue when they give you feedback

sections.heading: Follow through, and know your limits
sections.body:
What makes one-on-ones valuable is what happens afterwards. Note any action you agreed to, such as "I'll ask IT about your laptop" or "I'll speak to the regional manager about the training seat", and report back next time, even if the answer is no.

Keep what is shared confidential unless there is a safety, legal or policy concern, and be honest about that limit. If someone mentions serious stress, a health issue or a personal crisis, listen with care, but you are not a counsellor. Point them to the right support, such as HR or any employee assistance programme your company offers.
do: Write down your actions and report back
Point people to HR or other support when needed
dont: Promise total confidentiality you cannot keep

takeaways: A one-on-one is the team member's time, not a status update.
Hold it regularly and reschedule rather than cancel.
Use a light structure: their topics, your topics, actions.
Ask open, specific questions and then listen.
Follow through on every action you agree to.
quiz: What is the main purpose of a one-on-one?
To collect detailed status updates on every task and deadline the person has
To check attendance and log-in times
To give the team member time to raise concerns, get help and discuss growth
To review the team's overall targets
Status updates belong in trackers; one-on-ones are for the person.
You have had to cancel your one-on-one with Rohit three weeks in a row. What message does this likely send?
That he is not a priority for you
That his work is going so well it needs no discussion
That you trust him completely
Nothing, as long as you send an apology
Repeated cancellations signal low priority; reschedule instead.
Which question is most likely to get a useful answer?
"Everything okay?"
"Any issues?"
"All good with the project?"
"Is anything slowing you down that I could help remove?"
Specific, open questions invite real answers.
In a 30-minute one-on-one, who should usually do most of the talking?
You, because you have more context
The team member
It should be split exactly 50-50
Whoever is more senior in the conversation
It is primarily their meeting.
Your team member says your last-minute requests make her week stressful. What should you do?
Explain in detail why those requests were unavoidable at the time
Change the subject to her pending work
Thank her, ask for an example, and discuss what could change
Say other team members don't seem to mind
Responding without defensiveness keeps honest feedback coming.
In your last one-on-one you promised to ask about a training seat. The answer was no. What should you do?
Report back honestly in the next one-on-one and discuss alternatives
Avoid mentioning it unless she asks
Say you are still waiting to hear back, so she stays hopeful a bit longer
Keep asking until the answer changes
Following up, even with a no, builds trust.
A team member shares that he is under heavy personal stress. What is the best response?
Tell him to keep personal matters out of work
Promise to sort out all his problems yourself
Ignore it and move on to the agenda
Listen with care and point him to HR or available support
Managers can care and help connect people to support without acting as counsellors.
How often should you plan a longer conversation about career goals?
Never — that's HR's job
Every few weeks, as a dedicated session
Only during the annual appraisal
Only if the person seems unhappy or threatens to resign
Career conversations rarely happen unless you plan for them.
What is a good way to keep track of one-on-one topics?
Rely on memory for both of you
Ask HR to keep minutes
A shared running agenda that either person can add to
Record each meeting on your phone without telling them
A shared list keeps both people prepared and topics from being forgotten.
Your field sales team member is rarely in the office. What is a sensible approach?
Skip one-on-ones until he is back in the office for a full day
Do it by text message only, since he is busy with clients all day
Hold it on a call while he is driving between client meetings
Fix a regular video or phone slot at a time he is not travelling
A regular, focused slot works even for remote staff; avoid distracted or unsafe settings.

scenarios.title: The one-word answers
scenarios.situation: In every one-on-one, Nikita, who joined your Chennai team six months ago, says "All good" and the meeting ends in five minutes. Her output has dipped slightly in the last month.

options.text: Ask more specific, open questions — "What's taking most of your energy this week?" — and share that you've noticed a small dip and want to help.
options.feedback: Better questions and a gentle, specific observation give her an easy way to open up.

options.text: Cancel her one-on-ones since she has nothing to discuss.
options.feedback: This removes the one space where an issue could surface, just when output is dipping.

options.text: Tell her directly that her output has dropped and she needs to improve by next month.
options.feedback: It is honest, but without first understanding the cause it may feel like a warning rather than support.

scenarios.title: Feedback about you
scenarios.situation: In a one-on-one, Arjun says, "Honestly, when you reply to my updates in the group with just 'ok', it feels like you don't care about the work." You think you were just being efficient.

options.text: Explain that you are very busy and short replies are just your style.
options.feedback: Defending yourself tells Arjun that honest feedback is not welcome.

options.text: Thank him for telling you, ask what kind of response would be more useful, and agree to try it.
options.feedback: Accepting feedback calmly and acting on it shows the one-on-one is a real two-way space.

options.text: Say thanks and move on to your agenda.
options.feedback: Not defensive, but without exploring it or changing anything, Arjun may wonder whether it mattered.

options.text: Ask whether others in the team feel the same way.
options.feedback: This shifts the focus away from his experience and can feel like you are checking whether to believe him.

scenarios.title: The urgent clash
scenarios.situation: Your regional head calls a meeting that clashes with your weekly one-on-one with Farhan. You have already moved his slot once this month.

options.text: Cancel Farhan's one-on-one; he will understand.
options.feedback: A second change in a month without explanation tells him he is a low priority.

options.text: Message Farhan, explain the clash, and move the one-on-one to later the same day or the next morning.
options.feedback: Rescheduling quickly, with a reason, protects the meeting and the trust behind it.

options.text: Ask Farhan whether he minds skipping it this week.
options.feedback: Respectful, but it puts the burden on him; offering a new slot is better.

cards.title: One-on-ones that matter
cards.text: A one-on-one is your team member's time, not a status update. Learn how to make these short meetings the most useful 30 minutes of their week.

cards.title: Reschedule, don't cancel
cards.text: Pick a recurring weekly or fortnightly slot. Cancelling three times says: you're not a priority.
cards.bad: Sorry, something urgent came up. Let's skip this week.
cards.good: A review clashes with our slot. Can we do 4 pm today instead?

cards.title: A simple 30-minute flow
cards.text: Their topics first, then yours, then actions. Keep a shared running agenda either person can add to.
cards.example: 15 min their topics · 10 min yours · 5 min who does what by when

cards.title: Ask questions that open up
cards.text: Specific, open questions get real answers. Then pause and let them think.
cards.good: Is anything slowing you down that I could help remove?

cards.title: Take feedback without arguing
cards.text: If you get defensive once, you may never hear honest feedback again.
cards.bad: That's just my style; I'm busy.
cards.good: Thanks for telling me. What would be more useful?

cards.title: After every one-on-one
cards.text: Tap each one as you do it.
items: Write down the actions you promised
Report back next time, even if it's a no
Keep what was shared confidential
Plan a career chat every few weeks
cards.tip: Serious stress or a crisis? Listen, then point them to HR or support.

cards.title: You've got it!
cards.text: Five habits for better one-on-ones:

lessons.title: Leading Without the Title
lessons.summary: Show leadership in your first job before you manage anyone. You will learn how to own your work, take sensible initiative, influence peers and make your interest in leading visible.

sections.heading: Leadership starts before the promotion
sections.body:
Most people are promoted to manager because they were already acting like one. Managers notice who takes ownership, helps others and solves problems without being chased. The title usually comes after the behaviour, not before.

You may already have done this. Coordinating a college fest, keeping a placement-prep group on track, or getting a group project submitted when two members went silent all involved leading without formal authority.

In your first job, leadership is less about giving instructions and more about being someone others can rely on, learn from and work with. That reputation builds quietly over months.
do: Notice where you already lead informally
dont: Wait for a title before taking responsibility

sections.heading: Be completely reliable first
sections.body:
Nobody follows a person who misses deadlines. Before anything else, become the person whose work is done on time, checked and complete. This is the foundation every other leadership behaviour stands on.

Reliability also means flagging problems early. "I'll need one more day for the reconciliation because two branches haven't sent data; I've followed up with both" is far better than silence until the deadline. Your manager can plan around a known delay; a surprise causes trouble.

Keep a simple list of what you have promised and to whom. When you say "I'll send it by evening", treat it as a commitment.
do: Flag delays early with a reason and a plan
Track every promise you make
dont: Go silent when you are falling behind

sections.heading: Take initiative the right way
sections.body:
Initiative means noticing a problem and doing something useful about it. In your first months, you see things that experienced staff no longer notice. For example, new joiners in your Mumbai back-office team struggle with the same five process questions every month.

The right move is to propose, not to impose. "I noticed new joiners keep asking the same questions. Could I put together a one-page guide? I can draft it this week for you to review." This respects your manager's role and gives you a clear, visible piece of work.

Avoid overstepping. Changing a shared process, contacting a senior client or messaging another department's head without checking first can create problems, even with good intentions.
do: Bring a problem with a proposed solution
Ask before changing shared processes
dont: Complain about problems without suggesting anything
Contact senior stakeholders without checking

sections.heading: Influence peers without authority
sections.body:
With colleagues at your own level, you cannot instruct; you can only influence. The most effective way is to be genuinely helpful. Share a useful Excel shortcut, explain a process to the newer joiner, or cover for someone during an emergency. People remember who helped them.

When you need something from peers, ask rather than tell, and explain why. "Could you send your section by Wednesday? I need two days to combine and check everything before Friday" works better than "Send it by Wednesday."

If you are asked to coordinate a small group task, such as an induction batch presentation, run it well: agree who does what, set a check-in date, share credit by name at the end. Small group tasks like this are often where managers first notice leadership.
do: Help others without keeping score
Explain the why when you ask peers for something
dont: Take credit for group work

sections.heading: Make your ambition visible, calmly
sections.body:
Your manager cannot read your mind. If you want to lead one day, say so in a one-on-one: "In a year or two I'd like to take on team responsibility. What should I work on to get there?" Then ask for a small stretch task, such as training a new joiner or running a weekly huddle.

Show interest through behaviour, not lobbying. Office politics, speaking badly about colleagues or constantly asking "When will I be promoted?" damage your chances. Steady ownership, helpfulness and growth make the case for you.

Finally, learn from the managers around you. Notice what good ones do when a client escalates or a deadline slips, and what you would do differently.
do: Tell your manager you want to grow into leading
Ask for one small stretch task
dont: Lobby for promotion or play office politics

takeaways: Leadership behaviour usually comes before the title.
Be completely reliable and flag delays early.
Bring problems with a proposed solution, and check before acting.
Influence peers by helping and explaining the why.
Tell your manager you want to lead and ask for a stretch task.
quiz: You will miss a deadline because two branches have not sent data. What should you do?
Wait until the deadline and then explain what went wrong
Submit incomplete work without mentioning the gaps to anyone
Tell your manager early, explain why, and share your plan
Ask a colleague to tell the manager for you
Early, clear flags let your manager plan around the delay.
You notice new joiners keep asking the same process questions. What is the best initiative?
Offer to draft a one-page guide for your manager to review
Rewrite the official process document without telling anyone
Complain in the team group that onboarding is poor
Ignore it, since it is not your job
Proposing a solution and checking first shows initiative without overstepping.
How do you best influence peers when you have no authority over them?
Remind them you have better exam scores
Escalate to your manager every time they are slow to respond
Copy senior people on emails to add pressure
Help them genuinely and explain the why behind your requests
Helpfulness and clear reasons build influence among equals.
Which request to a peer is most likely to work?
"Send your section by Wednesday."
"Could you send your section by Wednesday? I need two days to check it before Friday."
"Manager wants it, so send it fast."
"Whenever you get time, send it."
A polite ask with a reason and deadline gets cooperation.
You want to grow into a team lead role. What is the best first step?
Ask your manager what you should work on and request a small stretch task
Ask your manager about your promotion every week until it finally happens
Point out a colleague's mistakes in meetings so that you look better
Wait quietly and hope that someone senior eventually notices your work
Stating your goal and asking for a stretch task makes your ambition visible the right way.
You coordinated your induction batch's group presentation and it went well. What should you do at the end?
Present it as mainly your own work, since you coordinated it
Thank the group and credit each person's part by name
Say nothing and move on
Tell your manager who did the least
Sharing credit builds trust and is itself a leadership signal.
Which action risks overstepping in your first month?
Offering to help a colleague with a backlog
Suggesting an improvement to your manager
Emailing a senior client directly about a change without checking
Sharing a useful Excel shortcut with the team
Contacting senior stakeholders without checking can create problems, even with good intentions.
Why does reliability matter so much for future leaders?
Because it is easier than being creative
Because managers only care about attendance
Because it guarantees a promotion within your first year at the company
Because people do not follow someone they cannot depend on
Reliability is the foundation of trust; no behaviour guarantees promotion.
Which past experience is a genuine example of leading without a title?
Getting a group project submitted when two members went silent
Scoring the highest marks in your batch in the final semester exams
Attending every single lecture and lab session in college
Getting a high CGPA and a scholarship for academic merit
Leadership involves getting results with and through others.
A colleague asks for help with a task during your busy week. What shows leadership?
Refuse, because helping won't be noticed
Help only if your manager is watching
Agree to everything they ask and miss your own deadline as a result
Help where you can, and be clear about what you can't fit in
Helpfulness is valuable, but so is honesty about your own commitments.

scenarios.title: The silent group member
scenarios.situation: Your induction batch at a Noida bank has to present a process-improvement idea in four days. Of five members, Vivek hasn't replied in the WhatsApp group for two days, and the others are getting irritated.

options.text: Call Vivek privately, check if he is okay, and agree on a smaller, specific part he can finish by Thursday.
options.feedback: It shows care, avoids public blame and gets the work back on track with a clear task.

options.text: Post in the group: "Some people aren't contributing — we'll tell the trainer."
options.feedback: Public blame and threats damage the team and rarely produce work.

options.text: Quietly divide Vivek's part among the other four.
options.feedback: It protects the deadline, but without speaking to Vivek you don't know why he went quiet or include him.

options.text: Tell the trainer that Vivek is not contributing.
options.feedback: Escalating before trying to talk to him skips the obvious first step.

scenarios.title: Your good idea
scenarios.situation: Three months into your job at an insurance company's Pune office, you realise the daily claims tracker could be updated automatically with a simple Excel formula, saving each colleague about 20 minutes a day.

options.text: Change the shared tracker tonight so everyone sees the improvement tomorrow.
options.feedback: Changing a shared tool without checking risks breaking something others depend on.

options.text: Show your manager a working copy, explain the time saved, and offer to roll it out if they agree.
options.feedback: Proposing with evidence respects the process and makes your contribution visible.

options.text: Use the formula in your own copy and keep the time saved for yourself.
options.feedback: It is safe, but a chance to help the whole team and show initiative is missed.

scenarios.title: Asking to lead
scenarios.situation: You have been in your role for a year and consistently meet targets. You'd like to lead a team someday, but your manager has never raised it in your one-on-ones.

options.text: Wait; if you are good enough, your manager will offer it.
options.feedback: Managers may not know your goal unless you say it.

options.text: Tell colleagues you deserve a promotion and hope word reaches your manager.
options.feedback: Indirect lobbying looks political and may harm your reputation.

options.text: Raise it in your next one-on-one: say you'd like to lead in future, ask what to work on, and offer to train the next new joiner.
options.feedback: It is direct, shows readiness to learn and suggests a concrete stretch step.

options.text: Email your manager asking whether you can be considered for team lead.
options.feedback: Clear about your goal, but a conversation that asks what to work on is more open and constructive.

cards.title: Lead before you're the boss
cards.text: People are usually promoted because they already act like leaders. Learn how to show leadership in your first job — no title needed.

cards.title: Flag delays early
cards.text: Reliability is the foundation. A known delay can be planned around; a surprise can't.
cards.bad: (Silence until the deadline) Sorry, it's not ready.
cards.good: I'll need one more day — two branches haven't sent data. I've followed up with both.

cards.title: Propose, don't impose
cards.text: Spot a problem? Bring a solution and check before changing anything shared.
cards.bad: Onboarding here is so badly organised.
cards.good: New joiners keep asking the same questions. Could I draft a one-page guide for you to review?

cards.title: Ask peers, and say why
cards.text: You can't instruct equals — you can only influence them.
cards.good: Could you send it by Wednesday? I need two days to check everything before Friday.

cards.title: Help, and share the credit
cards.text: Help others without keeping score. When a group task goes well, name each person's part.
cards.example: Thanks, Neha, for the data and Vivek for the slides — that made it work.

cards.title: Make your ambition visible
cards.text: Tap each one as you do it.
items: Tell your manager you'd like to lead someday
Ask what to work on to get there
Request one small stretch task
Watch how good managers handle tough moments
cards.tip: Skip the lobbying and office politics.

cards.title: You've got it!
cards.text: Five ways to lead without the title:

lessons.title: Leading a Sales or Advisory Team Ethically
lessons.summary: Lead relationship managers or advisers so that targets are met through suitable advice, not mis-selling. You will learn how to set balanced goals, coach client conversations, handle complaints and escalate compliance concerns.

sections.heading: Your team copies what you reward
sections.body:
As a new branch or team manager in a bank, AMC distributor or advisory firm, you sit between business targets from above and clients who trust your team with their savings. That position carries real influence: your team will learn far more from what you celebrate than from any compliance training.

If the only thing praised in the morning huddle is the day's highest sale, people hear "sell at any cost." If you also recognise the relationship manager who talked a 62-year-old client out of a high-risk product that did not fit her needs, they hear that suitability matters here.

Targets are a normal part of financial services. The ethical question is not whether to have them but how they are met. Say it plainly and often: "I want the numbers, but only from the right product for the right client."
do: Recognise good advice, not just big sales
Repeat that suitability comes first
dont: Celebrate only the highest number of the day

sections.heading: Set goals that do not reward mis-selling
sections.body:
Look beyond sales volume when you review your team. Useful quality signals include complete risk-profiling and need-analysis records, complaints received, early surrenders, redemptions or cancellations soon after a sale, and feedback from client reviews. A spike in policies cancelled within the free-look period or funds redeemed within weeks is a warning sign.

Discuss how a number was achieved, not just whether it was. "Your SIP numbers are strong this month. Walk me through two of those clients: what were their goals and why this fund?" makes quality part of every review.

Be careful about pushing particular products because they pay higher commission or because there is a contest running. Recommendations must follow the client's needs, risk profile and time horizon. Clients should also be told, in line with applicable rules, what they are paying and how the adviser or distributor is paid.
do: Track complaints and early exits alongside sales
Ask how each number was achieved
dont: Push a product because it pays more commission
Let contests override client needs

sections.heading: Coach the client conversation
sections.body:
The best way to raise both quality and results is to coach real conversations. Join client meetings or listen to calls with consent and in line with company policy, then give feedback using specific examples.

Watch for risky phrases. "This fund is as safe as an FD", "Guaranteed 12% returns" or "This NFO will double your money" are misleading. Coach replacements: "Mutual funds carry market risk; this one's risk level is moderately high, and returns are not guaranteed. Past performance doesn't promise future returns."

Help your team ask better questions before recommending anything: What is this money for? When will you need it? How would you feel if it fell 15% in a bad year? A relationship manager who understands the client's goal can recommend with confidence and is less tempted to oversell.
do: Coach with specific phrases from real calls
Train needs-first questions
dont: Let "guaranteed" or "as safe as an FD" go uncorrected

sections.heading: Handle complaints properly
sections.body:
When a client complains, your first job is to listen and understand, not to defend your team. "I understand you were told this policy had no lock-in. Let me look into exactly what happened and come back to you by Thursday" is calm and specific.

Then collect the facts: the documents signed, the risk profile, call notes and what the team member says. Follow your firm's grievance process and timelines, and record the complaint in the official system. Do not try to settle it quietly to protect your branch's numbers.

After resolving it, look for patterns. If three complaints in a quarter mention the same product or the same explanation, that is a coaching or process issue, not bad luck.
do: Acknowledge, investigate and respond by a stated date
Log every complaint in the official system
dont: Defend your team before you know the facts
Hide complaints to protect branch numbers

sections.heading: Escalate compliance concerns
sections.body:
Sometimes you will see something worse than a weak conversation: a signature that looks forged, transactions done without a client's instruction, a senior colleague pressuring the team to switch clients' investments for commission, or a target that can only be met by mis-selling.

Do not ignore it or handle it quietly. Write down what you saw with dates and facts, and escalate through your compliance team or the firm's whistle-blower or ethics channel. Raising a concern in good faith is part of your job as a manager.

Treat the people involved fairly. Do not accuse anyone in front of the team or decide guilt yourself; let the proper process establish the facts. And if you yourself are pressured to look the other way, remember that the client's interest and your professional registration both depend on getting this right.
do: Record facts and escalate through compliance or ethics channels
Let the formal process decide
dont: Cover up a problem to protect a team member
Accuse someone publicly before facts are established

takeaways: Your team copies what you praise — recognise suitable advice, not just sales.
Review complaints, early exits and needs-analysis quality alongside volume.
Coach real conversations and correct any promise of returns.
Handle complaints by listening, investigating and logging them properly.
Escalate serious concerns through compliance; never cover them up.
quiz: Which huddle message best supports ethical selling?
"Whoever sells the most today gets an early leave."
"I want the numbers, but only from the right product for the right client."
"Focus on the product with the best payout this month."
"Don't overthink suitability; clients are adults and can decide for themselves."
It sets the target and the standard for how it is met.
Which signal most strongly suggests possible mis-selling in your team?
A rise in sales during a festive season
A relationship manager with many loyal, repeat clients over the years
Many policies cancelled within the free-look period
More clients asking for annual reviews
Early cancellations or redemptions often mean the product did not fit the client.
A relationship manager tells a client, "This fund is as safe as an FD." How should you coach him?
Explain that funds carry market risk and practise an accurate risk explanation
Tell him it is fine to say this as long as the fund has performed well recently
Ask him to say it only to experienced investors
Let it go if the client did not complain
Comparing market-linked products to FDs misleads clients about risk.
A sales contest offers a bonus for a specific product. A client's needs fit a different product. What should your team member recommend?
The contest product, since the bonus helps the team
Both, and let the client choose randomly
The contest product, with a small discount
The product that fits the client's needs and risk profile
Recommendations must follow suitability, not incentives.
A client complains she was told a policy had no lock-in. What should you do first?
Remind her firmly that she signed the documents and must have read every clause
Assure her the team member would never say that
Acknowledge her concern and commit to investigating and replying by a date
Offer a gift to settle the matter quietly
Listening first and committing to a fact-based response is fair to both the client and the team.
Why log every complaint in the official system?
To ensure proper handling within timelines and to spot patterns
To build a detailed case against the team members who were involved
Only because auditors may check
There is no need if it is resolved quickly
Recording complaints supports fair resolution and reveals recurring issues.
In a monthly review, which question best checks quality?
"Why weren't your numbers higher than last month, given how strong the market was?"
"Can you beat your colleague next month?"
"How many calls did you make?"
"Walk me through two of these clients — their goals and why this fund?"
Asking how a sale was made makes suitability part of every review.
You notice a client's signature on a switch form looks very different from earlier forms. What should you do?
Ask the team member to quietly get the form re-signed by the client
Record the facts and escalate through compliance
Accuse the team member in the next huddle
Ignore it unless the client complains
Possible forgery is serious; escalate through the proper channel and let the process decide.
Which question best helps an adviser understand a client before recommending?
"Shall I put you in our top-performing fund?"
"How much can you invest today?"
"When will you need this money, and what is it for?"
"Do you want returns like your friend got?"
Goal and time horizon are core to a suitable recommendation.
A senior colleague asks your team to move clients between funds mainly to earn fresh commission. What should you do?
Do it, since a senior has asked
Do it only for the clients who are unlikely to notice the switch
Ask the team to decide individually
Decline and raise it through compliance or the ethics channel
Churning for commission harms clients; escalation in good faith is the manager's duty.

scenarios.title: The top seller with complaints
scenarios.situation: Rahul is your branch's top mutual fund seller this quarter. You notice that four of his clients redeemed within two months, and one has complained that she was told returns were "almost guaranteed." Your regional head is about to name Rahul star performer.

options.text: Let the recognition go ahead and talk to Rahul about it next quarter.
options.feedback: Rewarding him now, with a complaint pending, tells the whole team that numbers matter more than honest advice.

options.text: Tell your regional head about the complaint and the early redemptions, investigate the facts, and coach Rahul on accurate risk explanation.
options.feedback: It is transparent upward, fair to Rahul through a proper process, and addresses the behaviour directly.

options.text: Speak to Rahul privately and ask him to be more careful in future.
options.feedback: Addressing it is right, but without investigating and informing your head, the complaint and recognition issue are left unresolved.

options.text: Announce in the huddle that misleading clients will not be tolerated.
options.feedback: A general warning does not deal with the specific complaint and can feel like public shaming.

scenarios.title: Month-end pressure
scenarios.situation: It is the 28th and your team is 20% short of target. A team member suggests calling elderly fixed-deposit customers whose FDs are maturing and moving them into a high-commission market-linked product, "because they don't ask many questions."

options.text: Agree, but ask the team to fill risk profiles first.
options.feedback: Risk profiling helps, but the plan still targets clients because they are less likely to question, which is not acceptable.

options.text: Reject the idea clearly, explain why targeting clients who ask fewer questions is wrong, and plan suitable outreach based on client needs.
options.feedback: It sets the ethical line firmly and still gives the team a legitimate way to work towards the target.

options.text: Go ahead, since FD customers could benefit from higher returns.
options.feedback: Selecting clients for being less likely to question a sale is mis-selling, whatever the product's potential.

scenarios.title: The angry client at the branch
scenarios.situation: A client walks into your branch upset, saying an insurance plan sold to him last year was described as an investment with no risk, and now he cannot get his money back without a loss. The relationship manager who sold it insists she explained everything.

options.text: Tell the client that he signed the documents, so the matter is closed.
options.feedback: Dismissing the client without checking the facts damages trust and ignores the possibility of mis-selling.

options.text: Believe the client and tell the relationship manager she will face action.
options.feedback: Deciding guilt before reviewing the facts is unfair to your team member.

options.text: Listen calmly, log the complaint, review the documents and call notes, and give the client a date for a response through the grievance process.
options.feedback: It is respectful to the client, fair to the team member and follows the proper process.

options.text: Apologise and ask the relationship manager to call him later to sort it out.
options.feedback: The apology helps, but handing it back without logging or investigating may leave the complaint unresolved.

cards.title: Lead a team clients can trust
cards.text: Your team learns more from what you praise than from any compliance training. Learn how to hit targets through suitable advice — never mis-selling.

cards.title: Praise the right behaviour
cards.text: If you only celebrate the biggest sale, people hear: sell at any cost.
cards.bad: Top seller today gets early leave!
cards.good: I want the numbers — but only from the right product for the right client.

cards.title: Look beyond sales volume
cards.text: Track complaints, needs-analysis quality and early exits alongside sales. Ask how each number was achieved.
cards.example: Walk me through two of these SIP clients — their goals and why this fund?

cards.title: Correct risky promises
cards.text: Coach accurate risk language from real calls. Never let "guaranteed" slip by.
cards.bad: This fund is as safe as an FD.
cards.good: Mutual funds carry market risk; returns aren't guaranteed. This fund's risk level is moderately high.

cards.title: Listen before you defend
cards.text: Complaint? Acknowledge, investigate facts, log it, reply by a date.
cards.bad: You signed the form, so the matter is closed.
cards.good: Let me look into exactly what happened and come back to you by Thursday.

cards.title: If you spot a red flag
cards.text: Forged signature, unauthorised trade or pressure to churn? Tap each step.
items: Write down the facts and dates
Escalate to compliance or the ethics channel
Don't accuse anyone publicly
Never cover it up

cards.title: You've got it!
cards.text: Five rules for leading an ethical sales team:
